sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Hiiaka** ​(*hiiaka*) — ‌Hula, Magic, ‌Healing ​· patron ​goddess ​of Hawaiʻi ​— belongs ​to ‌the Polynesian ​tradition, ​where it ‌is catalogued ​under ‌the domain ​"Hula, Magic, ‌Healing". ​The name ​means ​"patron goddess ​of Hawaiʻi"[^1].

​**Hiiaka** ‌is the ​youngest ‌sister of ​the volcano-goddess ‌Pele: ​patroness of ‌the ​hula, guardian ‌of the ​hālau ​hula where ‌the dance ‌is ‌taught, and ​a ​healer whose ‌chants restore ​the ​dying. Her ‌story ​— an ​oath, a ‌quest, ​and a ‌betrayal between ​sisters ​— is ​the ​great romance ‌of the ‌Hawaiian ​Pele cycle.[^2]

‌PuniCodex ​records the ​canonical scholarly ‌spelling ‌**Hiiaka** and ‌serves its ‌temple ​at [its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/hiiaka/). ​The displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent ‌— a ​description ​computed from ​the displayed ‌form ​itself. The ​plain ​ASCII form ‌*hiiaka* contains ​the ‌same letters: ​no recovered ‌diacritics ​or special ‌encoding ‌is claimed. ​The work ​here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​modern Polynesian ​orthographies; ​macron ​usage follows ​each ‌tradition’s ​reference dictionaries. ​Etymologically ‌the ​name means ‌"patron ​goddess ‌of Hawaiʻi"[^1].

​The ​canonical ​spelling **Hiiaka** ​matches ​the ‌conventional scholarly ​romanization. ‌The ​plain ASCII ‌form ​*hiiaka* ‌contains the ​same ‌letters, ​so no ​lost ‌diacritics ‌or encoding ‌transition ​is ​claimed. The ‌editorial ​work ​is to ‌fix ​one ​reviewed reference ‌spelling, ​preserve capitalization ‌and ​provenance, ​and keep ​the ​original ‌evidence visible. ‌The ​displayed ‌form is ​ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a description ‌computed ‌from ‌the displayed ​form ‌itself.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- ‌**h** → ​**H** ​— ​Same, capitalized
- ‌**i** ​→ ​**i** — ​Same
- ‌**i** ​→ **i** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**a** → ​**a** ‌— ‌Same
- **k** ​→ ​**k** ​— Same
- ​**a** ‌→ ‌**a** — ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/hiiaka/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**hiiaka** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Hiiaka.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Hiiaka" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Hiiaka" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"hiiaka" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Hiiaka ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Hiiaka ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous ‌writing ‌system ​is securely ​attested ​for ​individual ​polynesian ‌names. ​The ​form shown ‌is ​a ‌modern ​scholarly ‌transliteration.[^1]

​The ​form **Hiiaka** ​is ​therefore ​a ‌scholarly ​transliteration ‌rather ​than ‌an attested ​ancient ‌spelling; ​it ‌encodes ​the ​reconstructed ‌sound of ‌the ‌name ​for ​modern ‌use, ​and ​no mark ‌in ​it ​is ‌decorative.

​Pre-contact ‌Hawaiʻi ​had ​no writing; ​the ​name ‌comes ‌down ​in ‌the ​Latin-based Hawaiian ​orthography ‌developed ‌after ‌the ‌1820s. ​The ‌fuller traditional ​spelling ​is ​**Hiʻiaka**, ‌with ​ʻokina ​(glottal ​stop) ‌marking the ​consonant ​between ​the ‌vowels ​and ‌kahakō ​(macron) marking ‌the ​long ‌ī; ‌the ​canonical ​temple ​restoration is ​the ‌normalized ‌form ​**Hiiaka**.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Hiiaka ‌place ​hula, magic, ​healing ​at the ​center ​of ‌a living ​mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins (Myth)

​Hiiaka ‌appears in ​polynesian ‌tradition ​as hula, ​magic, ​healing. The ​name's ​meaning, ‌"patron goddess ​of ‌Hawaiʻi", ​shapes the ‌narratives ​told about ‌this ​figure.

### ‌Worship and ​Memory ​(Cult)

Devotees ‌and ‌later ‌tradition-keepers preserved ​Hiiaka ​in ‌ritual, text, ​and ​iconography, ensuring ‌the ​name ​survived into ‌the ​modern scholarly ‌record.

​The ​myths of ​Hiiaka ​survive in ‌fragments, ‌summaries, ​and later ‌retellings. ​Each ​version reflects ‌the ‌interests of ‌its ‌tellers ​— poets, ‌priests, ​philosophers, and ​scholars. ​The ‌PuniCodex entry ​does ​not ​privilege a ‌single ​version; it ​gathers ​the ‌attestations so ​that ‌readers can ​compare ‌them. ​The restoration ‌Hiiaka ‌gives ​the figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Hiiaka ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Polynesian ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Hiiaka, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​hula ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Hiʻiaka ​is the ‌myth ‌of loyalty ​tested ​by ​power. She ​is ​the youngest, ‌the ​carried one, ​the ‌sister ​whose gifts ‌— ​dance, chant, ‌healing ​— are ​the ​gentle ​arts, and ​the ‌story gives ​her ‌the one ​role ‌the ​gentle arts ‌dread: ​the enforcer ‌of ​another's desire. ​Her ‌oath ‌to Pele ‌sends ​her across ​an ‌ocean of ​islands ​to ‌kill monsters ​and ​raise the ‌dead; ​and the ‌same ​oath ends ​with ​her ​friend burned ‌and ‌her own ​goddess ‌against her. ​The ​myth's ‌wisdom is ‌that ‌devotion and ‌obedience ​are not ‌the ​same, ​and that ​the ‌hearth that ​raised ​you can ​also ‌demand ​what it ​has ​no right ‌to ​burn. Every ‌hālau ​that ‌chants to ​her ‌chooses the ‌gentler ​half of ​that ​lesson: ​serve the ‌love, ‌not the ​fire.[^1]
